sources.title: TodoMVC behavior reference: precise functional contract

model.vision: A personal todo list a small team can rely on to capture, finish, and clear their work.

objectives.statement: Let a team member capture a task the moment it occurs to them, and correct or discard it later without re-entering it.
Give each person an at-a-glance, always-accurate count of what is still left to do.
Let people mark work done or not done, individually or all at once, as their plans change.
Keep the list uncluttered by letting people sweep away finished work and review only the slice of the list they care about.
Guarantee that a person's list is never lost between visits, so the team can trust it as their record of outstanding work.
Let the team's existing agent tooling and embedded workspaces work the same list the person sees, so tasks are never re-keyed across tools.
Be usable by a small team from the day after delivery.

model.mission: Deliver the classic, well-known todo experience exactly as people already expect it, with every list held durably by the team rather than in a person's browser. Offer that same list identically to people and to the team's agent tooling, so however someone reaches it they see and change one trustworthy record.

items.definition: A person on the team who keeps their own todo list and works it day to day.
The team's existing automated assistants that act on a person's todo list on their behalf, seeing and changing the same list the person does.
Another team tool that hosts the todo experience inside itself, so a person can work their list without leaving that tool.
A single task on a person's list, consisting of its wording (title) and whether it is done.
The ordered collection of todos belonging to one person, in the order they were captured.
The free-text wording that says what a todo is; never blank.
The state of a todo that has been marked done; a todo that is not completed is active.
The state of a todo that is still left to do (not completed).
Add a new, active todo to the end of the list from wording the person supplies; blank wording captures nothing.
Change an existing todo's title in place; rewording to blank discards the todo, and abandoning a reword leaves the original title untouched.
Remove one todo from the list regardless of whether it is done, leaving every other todo untouched.
Mark one todo done, or mark it not done again, without affecting any other todo.
In one action, mark every todo done — or, when every todo is already done, mark every todo not done.
In one action, remove every completed todo from the list, leaving active todos untouched; has no effect when nothing is completed.
Look at the list through a chosen view — all todos, only active, or only completed — without changing any todo.
The count of active todos on the whole list, always current and independent of which view is being shown.
Business activity: the person's chosen slice of the list — All, Active, or Completed; choosing one changes only what is shown and is always visibly indicated.
Business activity: the rule that decides what Toggle All does — if every todo is completed, uncomplete all; otherwise complete all.
Business activity: the rule that a title must contain visible text; blank or whitespace-only wording never becomes or remains a todo.
Business activity: counting the todos on the whole list that are not completed, recomputed after every change that affects which todos are active.
Resource access: fetch a person's whole todo list, with each todo's title and completed state, in captured order.
Resource access: durably record a new todo at the end of a person's list.
Resource access: durably record a changed title or completed state for an existing todo.
Resource access: durably remove one or more named todos from a person's list.
The team-held, durable record of every person's todo list, which survives the person closing the app, restarting their device, or the service restarting.

items.name: Operation-access-channel volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the channel through which a caller invokes the list operations (Capture, Reword, Discard, Toggle, Toggle All, Clear Completed, Retrieve). Today the same operations have to be reachable at the same time over an ordinary web API by Team Members' clients and over an MCP tool surface by Agent Tooling (brief; mission 'identically to people and to the team's agent tooling'; Objective 6). WHY VOLATILE: the set of channels is open-ended. Agent Tooling may want a different operation vocabulary (for example batch calls) than a browser does, and other team tools will want their own integration. LONGEVITY GROUNDING (no Required Behaviors are committed yet, so this entry cites the mission and is not traced): within roughly the last two years the team has added an MCP surface next to HTTP on 'everything else here', so it adopts about one new access channel every one to two years. At that rate a team tool with a three-plus-year life will gain at least one more channel. RISK: likelihood high, because there are two channels on day one and more are expected. Effect if unencapsulated: each channel re-implements Title Validation, the Aggregate Completion Rule and the Active Count Tally, those copies drift, and an agent and a person get different results from the same list. That breaks the mission's 'one trustworthy record'. The channel must therefore be a thin adapter that carries no list rules.

items.name: Presentation-host volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the host that renders the todo experience for a person. Today two hosts run it at the same time: a stand-alone web app in a browser, and Embedded Workspaces that host it as an MCP Apps UI. Each host imposes its own shell, sizing, theming, lifecycle and host-to-UI messaging bridge (brief; Objective 6). This is separate from the access channel because Agent Tooling has no presentation at all. WHY VOLATILE: the team says it embeds its other MCP-hosted UIs 'the same way', so more embedding hosts arrive as it adopts more tools, and different vendors' MCP Apps hosts already differ in what they support. LONGEVITY GROUNDING (untraced; no Required Behaviors are committed yet): MCP Apps-style embedding is less than two years old, and new hosts and host capabilities have shipped every few months. Over the tool's three-plus-year life the set of hosts will keep changing. RISK: likelihood high, with two hosts on day one. Effect if unencapsulated: screen logic forks per host, so the always-visible filter indication, Items Left and edit behavior can diverge between the browser and the embedded copy, and every new host means rewriting the experience rather than adding a shell.

items.name: Integration-protocol evolution volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the wire contracts that external tools use to reach the service: the MCP protocol and its MCP Apps extension, plus the versioned shape of the web API that other team tools bind to. WHY VOLATILE: these are moving standards that the same customer will be pushed to follow over time. LONGEVITY GROUNDING (untraced; no Required Behaviors are committed yet): since its November 2024 release, MCP has published dated revisions about two to four times a year (2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25). Those revisions changed the transport (SSE to streamable HTTP), the authorization model and structured tool output, and the Apps extension is younger and moving faster. At that rate the tool will see several breaking or additive revisions within its three-plus-year life. RISK: likelihood very high and recurring. Effect if unencapsulated: protocol specifics such as session handling, transport framing and capability negotiation leak into list workflow code, and every spec revision touches the core of the system instead of one adapter. This axis-1 change is independent of which channels exist (Operation-access-channel volatility).

items.name: Durable-storage volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the technology and location of the team-held Todo Store, which must survive the person closing the app, restarting the device, or restarting the service (Objective 5; the persistence contract says it must not be browser-local or in-memory). WHY VOLATILE: Objective 7 ('usable by a small team from the day after delivery') argues for the simplest durable store on day one. 'Built the way we build everything else here' will later pull the store onto the team's standard managed database, its backup regime and its hosting. LONGEVITY GROUNDING (untraced; no Required Behaviors are committed yet): internal team tools that launch on a minimal store usually migrate storage at least once in their first two to three years, as soon as they are adopted beyond a trial, and this brief describes exactly such a trial ('for our team to try out'). RISK: likelihood medium to high within the lifespan. Effect if unencapsulated: storage queries and schema details spread through every operation, a migration means rewriting all of them, and durability guarantees could silently change. Encapsulate behind the atomic business verbs the glossary already names (Retrieve List, Append Todo, Revise Todo, Remove Todos).

items.name: Person-identity volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how a caller establishes WHICH person's Todo List it is working. Every list belongs to one Team Member (glossary 'Todo List'), but today the evidence of identity differs by caller: a browser session for the web app, the host workspace's identity for an Embedded Workspace, and delegated credentials when Agent Tooling acts on someone's behalf (glossary 'Agent Tooling'; Objective 6). WHY VOLATILE: the set of identity schemes is open-ended and grows with every new host or agent. MCP's own authorization model has already been revised (OAuth-based authorization added and then reworked across 2025 revisions). LONGEVITY GROUNDING (untraced; no Required Behaviors are committed yet): the team's identity mechanisms for agent and embedded surfaces have changed at the pace of those MCP authorization revisions, about yearly, which falls well inside a three-plus-year life. Changes of identity provider over time are folded in here as the same underlying change. RISK: likelihood high. Effect if unencapsulated: identity checks are copied into every operation and channel, an agent can end up acting on the wrong person's list, and adding a host means touching every operation.

items.name: Concurrent-change propagation volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how a change made to a list through one consumer reaches the other consumers working the same list at the same time, and how simultaneous changes to the same todo are reconciled. Because a person and their Agent Tooling, and possibly an embedded copy, can work one list concurrently, Items Left must stay 'always accurate' (Objective 2) and everyone must 'see and change one trustworthy record' (mission; Objective 6). WHY VOLATILE: each consumer learns of change differently today. A browser can poll or hold a stream, an MCP Apps host relays notifications through its bridge, and agents simply re-read. The reconciliation policy (last writer wins or rejecting stale revisions) is open-ended. LONGEVITY GROUNDING (untraced; no Required Behaviors are committed yet): every new host and every MCP revision has added or changed a notification mechanism (resource subscriptions, list-changed notifications, Apps host messages), so this keeps changing at the same two-to-four-revisions-a-year rate. RISK: likelihood high once agents are used day to day. Effect if unencapsulated: freshness and conflict logic leaks into every client and into the store, so stale views can show a wrong Items Left count or overwrite an agent's change.

rejected.name: Aggregate Completion Rule change
rejected.reason: The Toggle All rule (uncomplete all if all are completed, otherwise complete all) is identical in every TodoMVC implementation, and the mission requires the experience 'exactly as people already expect it'. A change here would change what the product is, and a conditional expresses it fully.

rejected.name: Title Validation rule change
rejected.reason: The rule that blank or whitespace-only wording never becomes or remains a todo is the shared TodoMVC contract. Changing it is rare, and encapsulating it would only add a seam around one predicate.

rejected.name: Active Count Tally rule change
rejected.reason: Items Left is defined by the reference contract as the count of not-completed todos across the whole list, independent of the filter. Every competitor computes it identically.

rejected.name: Operation workflow sequencing
rejected.reason: The seven list operations each have a fixed one-step shape in the reference contract, and no objective expects new multi-step flows. The list workflow is the nature of this business, not a source of change.

rejected.name: View Filter set growth (filter by tag, due date, priority)
rejected.reason: The All/Active/Completed set is fixed by the contract. The attributes any new filter would need (tags, due dates, priorities) are explicitly out of scope, so planning for new filters designs for a different product.

rejected.name: Todo shape enrichment (due dates, priorities, tags)
rejected.reason: The behavior reference explicitly lists due dates, priorities and tags as out of scope and says they 'must not be assumed required'. Nothing in the mission asks for them.

rejected.name: Multi-user sharing of a list
rejected.reason: Lists are personal (vision: 'a personal todo list'), and multi-user sharing is explicitly out of scope. Agent Tooling acting on a person's behalf is covered by Person-identity volatility, not by sharing.

rejected.name: Manual reordering of todos
rejected.reason: The list stays in captured order, and drag-to-reorder is explicitly out of scope.

rejected.name: Undo/redo history
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope in the reference contract. Reword already supports abandoning an edit, which is all the contract asks for.

rejected.name: Offline sync of the list
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope. The mission deliberately holds the list in the team service rather than on the device, so offline replicas would be a different business.

rejected.name: Clear Completed retention (archive instead of remove)
rejected.reason: Clear Completed removes completed todos by contract, and no objective asks to keep or review cleared work. Archiving assumes a history feature that is out of scope.

rejected.name: Team size / load growth
rejected.reason: The brief is for a small team to try out. Designing now for organisation-scale load would serve a hypothetical customer, not the one in the brief.

rejected.name: Logging / reporting / analytics block
rejected.reason: Siren song (ch. 2 §3.6): no objective asks for reporting or analytics. The only aggregate the business needs is Items Left, which the list rules already cover. Adding the block by reflex is not justified.

rejected.name: Edit interaction gestures (double-click, Enter, Escape, blur)
rejected.reason: How a person starts, commits or abandons a Reword is a per-host binding inside the presentation, handled by simple conditional handling in each shell. It does not ripple beyond the screen.

rejected.name: Items Left wording and localisation ('1 item left' / 'n items left')
rejected.reason: Pluralisation and language of the counter are formatting choices made with a conditional or a string table. They do not change any business rule.

rejected.name: Hosting / deployment environment
rejected.reason: The founder fixes the house standard ('the way we build everything else here'). Where that standard runs the service (ports, hosts, environment) is configuration data. The part that really changes structurally, the store, is recorded as Durable-storage volatility.

rejected.name: Agent operation vocabulary (which operations agents get, batch calls)
rejected.reason: Folded into Operation-access-channel volatility: what each channel exposes is the same underlying change as which channel reaches the list operations.

rejected.name: Differences between MCP Apps host vendors
rejected.reason: Folded into Presentation-host volatility: one more host rendering the experience differently is the same underlying change.

rejected.name: Web API contract versioning
rejected.reason: Folded into Integration-protocol evolution volatility: a revision of the wire contract other team tools bind to is the same underlying change as an MCP spec revision.

rejected.name: Identity provider change over time (team SSO swap)
rejected.reason: Folded into Person-identity volatility: replacing how a person is identified is the same underlying change whether it happens across callers or over time. Keeping one entry also keeps the axes independent.

rejected.name: Authorization of agents acting on a person's behalf
rejected.reason: Folded into Person-identity volatility: delegated agent credentials are one of the identity schemes that entry encapsulates.

rejected.name: Simultaneous-edit conflict resolution policy
rejected.reason: Folded into Concurrent-change propagation volatility: reconciling two writers is the same underlying change as propagating one writer's change to the other consumers.

decisions.essenceRationale: Curating the list - bringing a task into the person's one trustworthy record the moment it occurs to them, and correcting or discarding it later without re-keying it (Objective 1) - is what every customer of a todo list buys, on every host and channel. It abstracts three customer-named operations (add, edit, delete) into one behavior: changing the CONTENT of the list under the Title Validation rule. It is nearly immutable (the TodoMVC contract has been identical for a decade) and it is differentiating here because the content change lands in the team-held record and reaches every other consumer at once, so a person and their Agent Tooling never diverge. Its flow crosses the Operation-access-channel, Integration-protocol, Person-identity, Durable-storage, Concurrent-change propagation and Presentation-host seams.

decisions.essenceRationale: Settling work - changing the done/not-done STATE of the list, one todo or all at once, and sweeping finished work away (Objectives 3 and 4) - is the second pillar of every todo list: capturing work is only half the value, closing it out is the other half. It abstracts toggle, toggle-all and clear-completed into one behavior governed by the Aggregate Completion Rule, a rule shared identically by all customers and unchanged across the reference contract's life. It is differentiating because the settlement is recorded durably in the team-held record and propagated to every concurrent consumer, so Items Left stays always accurate for the person and their agents alike. Its flow crosses the Person-identity, Durable-storage and Concurrent-change propagation seams, and the same access-channel and presentation-host seams as curation.

decisions.essenceRationale: Taking stock - seeing at a glance, on any return visit and through any host or agent, what is still outstanding and the slice of the list one cares about (Objectives 2, 4 and 5) - is why a person trusts the list as their record of outstanding work. It abstracts filtering, the items-left counter and persistence across visits into one read behavior that never changes data. It is shared by every customer and nearly immutable (All/Active/Completed and the whole-list active count are fixed by contract), and it is the differentiator of this mission: the list is held durably by the team, not in a browser, and is offered identically to people and to agents. Its flow crosses the Person-identity, Durable-storage, Presentation-host and Concurrent-change propagation (live subscription) seams.

verdicts.summary:
REVISE. First critique, so there is no prior delta. run_checks passes, so every finding below is doctrinal, not structural.

1. Concurrent-change propagation volatility is filed in the wrong layer, and its reconciliation half has no home anywhere. TodoListManager has only one entry in encapsulatesVolatilities: "Concurrent-change propagation volatility". The committed rationale for that volatility has two facets, and neither one is a workflow sequence. (a) Facet one is the reconciliation policy, folded in from "Simultaneous-edit conflict resolution policy": last-writer-wins versus rejecting stale revisions. That is a business-rule volatility, so it belongs in an Engine. No component or view realizes it today. ReviseTodo(todoId, title), ReviseTodo(todoId, completed: flipped) and RemoveTodos([todoId]) carry no revision or precondition. No step consults any policy before writing. ToggleAll does RetrieveList and then ReviseTodo(every todo...) with nothing that detects an interleaved change. The architecture claims a volatility it gives no seam. Fix: add an Engine that owns the reconciliation policy, for example a ChangeReconciliationEngine with a verb like ReconcileChange(observedRevision, currentRevision) → accept | stale. Have TodoListManager consult it before every write step in curate-the-list, settle-work and their variations. Let the RA write verbs carry the observed revision so the Engine has something to judge. This also clears the golden-ratio smell: right now there is 1 Manager and 0 Engines, and the draft records no justification for having no Engine. (b) Facet two is the per-consumer notification mechanism: a browser stream, MCP Apps bridge messages, an agent re-reading. The Manager does not hide that. It sits in the Clients and behind message-bus. State an explicit disposition for this facet: deferred to the pub/sub operational concept, with the per-host delivery in each Client. Then rewrite TodoListManager.encapsulates so it claims only what it actually hides. One honest wording is the sequence of reconcile, write, recount and propagate after every change. If the Manager then has no committed volatility left to cite, say so and deal with that openly. Do not keep a misfiled claim just to fill encapsulatesVolatilities.

2. The delivery seam for live views is only half drawn. take-stock-of-outstanding-work (step "sub") and work-the-list-inside-an-embedded-workspace (step "a2") draw WatchList → subscribe(ListChanged[owner]). Every change view draws publish(ListChanged[owner]). No relationship or label shows how a published ListChanged reaches the watching TodoWebApp or EmbeddedTodoApp. Both WatchList edges are plain sync calls, and a Manager→Client callback would be an upward call. Make the return path explicit and legal. For example, relabel both static Client→Manager edges and both view steps as "WatchList(owner) → stream of ListChanged until the view closes", and record in the operational-concepts deferral that the stream is fed from the bus subscription. Without that, the "always accurate" Items Left obligation (Objective 2) has no structural trigger.

3. The drive-the-list-from-agent-tooling view does not tell the truth. (a) Step a2 publish(ListChanged[owner]) fires for every operation in the a0 root, ReviewList included. A read changes nothing, so the edge draws a call the Manager would never make. Say in the label that it fires only for changes: "publish(ListChanged[owner]) — after a change operation; not on ReviewList". (b) The root edge promises "returns the refreshed list and Items Left", but this view never calls TallyItemsLeft. The sibling views capture-a-todo, discard-a-todo, mark-a-todo-done-or-not-done and the others all draw that tally as a separate step. That is the same work drawn at two granularities. If the committed activity node a1 is too coarse to show the tally separately, at least name TallyItemsLeft in the a1 label. (c) a1's "AppendTodo | ReviseTodo | RemoveTodos | RetrieveList — the verb the requested operation needs" is a gross-terms label. Name the mapping from operation to verb, for example Capture→AppendTodo, Reword→ReviseTodo/RemoveTodos, ToggleAll→RetrieveList+ReviseTodo, and so on.

Reservations to record but not blocking:
- Presentation-host volatility is claimed by both TodoWebApp and EmbeddedTodoApp. One thin shell per host is the right disposition. Record the two shells as a facet group so the double claim is ratified rather than implicit.
- ReviseTodo is used as a generic field-bag update (title in one place, completed in another, "every todo" in settle-work au/ac). The committed volatilities name these verbs, so I am not reopening that. But a bulk "every todo" write through a singular verb is the non-atomic ToggleAll that point 1 has to reconcile. Consider ReviseTodos or a dedicated SettleAll verb.
- RetrieveList's label "sliced by the View Filter" puts filter slicing in ResourceAccess, but the Resource hop reads all records. Decide where the filter applies and label it once.
- Single-surface use cases (switch-between-all-active-and-completed-views, find-the-list-intact-on-the-next-visit, work-the-list-inside-an-embedded-workspace) correctly omit the MCP path. No asymmetry defect there.

message-bus.content:
# MessageBus — Requirements scope note (C-message-bus)

**Layer:** Utility (`kind: utility`, contractKey `messageBus`). Cross-cutting infrastructure; encapsulates no business volatility of its own and carries no list rules.

**Volatility served:** *Concurrent-change propagation volatility* (allCustomersAtOneTime) — how a change made through one consumer reaches the other consumers working the same Todo List at the same time. The bus is the mechanism by which TodoListManager decouples the act of changing a list from the open-ended set of ways consumers learn of that change (browser stream/poll, MCP Apps host bridge, agent re-read). The reconciliation policy (last-writer-wins vs. stale-revision rejection) is NOT the bus's concern — it stays with the Manager/ResourceAccess.

## Responsibilities (each traced to the committed System)

1. **Carry ListChanged notifications scoped to one list owner.** Relationship `todo-list-manager → message-bus` (sync, "publish(ListChanged) / subscribe(ListChanged)"). Dynamic-view label: "publish(ListChanged[owner]) — to every other consumer of this list". Notifications are keyed by the owning Team Member; a publish for owner A must never reach a subscription for owner B.
   - Traced publish steps: curate-the-list (zb), settle-work (zb), capture-a-todo (t1), reword-a-todo (t1), discard-a-todo (a3), mark-a-todo-done-or-not-done (a3), mark-everything-done-at-once-and-undo-it (a3), sweep-away-finished-todos (a3), drive-the-list-from-agent-tooling (a2).
2. **Deliver to every *other* current consumer of that list.** Same publish label — fan-out to all live subscribers of the owner's list, so a person, their Agent Tooling, and an embedded copy converge on one trustworthy record (mission; Objective 2 'Items Left always accurate', Objective 6).
3. **Register a caller's live view as a subscriber.** Dynamic-view label "subscribe(ListChanged[owner]) — for the caller's live view" in take-stock-of-outstanding-work (sub) and work-the-list-inside-an-embedded-workspace (a2). The subscription lives as long as the caller's live view and must be releasable when that view ends.

Nothing beyond these three is in scope: the bus does not persist todos, does not validate titles, does not compute Items Left, does not authenticate (identity is established by the Manager via MemberIdentityAccess before the bus is touched), and does not know about HTTP/MCP/Apps transports — the clients' adapters translate bus deliveries into their own channel.

## Callers / consumers

- **Sole caller: `todo-list-manager`** (Manager layer), in both roles — publisher after a successful list mutation, and subscriber on behalf of a client's live view. No Client, Engine, or ResourceAccess calls the bus directly in the committed design; per the layer rules a Utility may be called from any layer, but no additional caller should be assumed.
- Indirect beneficiaries: `todo-web-app`, `embedded-todo-app`, `todo-mcp-server` (they receive change notice through the Manager's live-view path, not by talking to the bus).
- Outbound dependencies: none in the committed System (no relationship from message-bus to any component or Resource).

## Interaction treatment

- Both relationship and every dynamic-view call are marked **sync** from the Manager's side: the publish/subscribe *call* returns to the Manager promptly; delivery to other subscribers is decoupled from the publisher. Publishing must not block or fail the user's list mutation because a subscriber is slow, gone, or misbehaving — the mutation is already durably recorded in TodoStore before publish.
- The committed Deployment & Operations Model sets no scenario/scaling/infra knobs for a broker (all null), so no external broker Resource is designated; the day-one implementation target is in-process within the service, per Objective 7 (usable the day after delivery).

## Non-functional constraints

- **Maintainability:** generic over message type and topic key; zero dependency on todo domain types beyond what the Manager hands it. Small, testable in isolation with a fake subscriber; deterministic tests (no sleeps) for fan-out, owner isolation, and unsubscribe.
- **Extensibility:** swapping the in-process mechanism for a networked broker (multi-instance hosting, team standard infra) must not change the Manager's usage — that is precisely the propagation volatility. New consumer kinds (new embedding hosts, new MCP notification styles) must be addable without touching the bus.
- **Security / isolation:** strict per-owner scoping — cross-owner leakage would expose one Team Member's list to another (Person-identity volatility). The bus trusts the owner key it is given; it never derives identity itself. Notifications should carry minimal payload (signal of change, not necessarily list content) to limit exposure.
- **Reliability / resource hygiene:** concurrent-safe for simultaneous publishers and subscribers; abandoned subscriptions must be reclaimable (no goroutine/channel leaks when a browser tab or embedded host disappears); a slow subscriber must not starve others.
- **Delivery semantics:** at-most-once, best-effort is acceptable because consumers can always re-read the authoritative list (agents 'simply re-read'); loss must never corrupt state, only delay freshness.

## Scope sizing (Ch. 7)

10 effort-days, junior-developer, risk bucket 2. Beyond coding: concurrency test client (race detector), owner-isolation tests, lifecycle/leak tests, and integration with TodoListManager's live-view path. Risk of gold-plating: building durable queues, replay, or a broker adapter now — out of scope until operations designate one.

## Open questions for Detailed Design

1. What does a ListChanged notification carry — owner + revision marker only, or a change summary? (Bears on payload exposure and whether consumers must re-read.)
2. Does the publisher's own subscription receive its own publish ('every *other* consumer') — is self-suppression the bus's job or the Manager's?
3. Subscription lifetime: explicit release by the Manager vs. context/cancellation-bound; what happens on service restart (subscribers reconnect and re-read?).
4. Back-pressure policy for slow subscribers: drop, coalesce latest, or disconnect?
5. Should the topic abstraction be generic (any message type/key) now, or ListChanged-specific, given only one message type exists in the committed design?
6. Multi-instance hosting: confirm in-process is sufficient for the trial deployment, deferring a broker Resource to a future operational-concepts change.
